examples.name: Sample — a shaded rate map
paragraphs: A regional map of Italy shaded in three bands, one value printed in each region, a four-entry legend and a caption. The geography is decoration; the values are the content, so the map is a table. The map prints only values: each region is recognised from its outline, so the key column is marked data-recognised, and its header follows the caption's wording. Basilicata is printed white (n.d.) with no value, so it has no row; the caption states the gap. The table as it renders:

examples.name: Sample — a map that is entirely data, with no printed key
paragraphs: An observed-precipitation map: state outlines, and on top of them a dense scatter of numeric readings, colour-coded by value.

This is a data display wearing a map, so the test says table. But it is also the case where that answer stops being practical: the readings are positioned by latitude and longitude with no station names printed, so there is no key column to put them in. The readings sit at points, not in drawn regions, so there is nothing to recognise as a key: the legend text is transcribed, the map is described, and no table is built.

The legend block in the top-left — title, valid time, sources and a red "Data not fully quality controlled" caveat — is printed text and MUST survive whatever is done with the plotted values. The red colour is emphasis, not a value, and is not carried. The plotted readings are too small to transcribe reliably at this resolution and are not listed.

examples.name: Sample — a real map with a printed legend
paragraphs: An aerial map of well locations, colour-coded by concentration band, with a six-entry legend, a scale bar, a callout (610 ng/l), a state inset and a photograph. The positions are the content, so the map is described as an image with every legend entry and label transcribed. Expected boxes: the title, the subtitle, the map with its caption, the legend, the inset with its caption and the photograph with its caption.
